messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Network Engineer
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 44

At 33, she is a network engineer who is used to solving problems by tracing them to their source. In her work, outages have causes, systems can be mapped, and with enough persistence a failure can usually be isolated and repaired. What happened with her son does not fit that logic, and that remains one of the hardest things for her to live with.

She speaks about the beginning of it in a flat, careful way, as if reading from an incident log. Her son is still very young when he becomes suddenly and frighteningly ill. At first she tells herself it is probably a virus, one of the ordinary childhood illnesses parents swap stories about. Then his breathing changes. His skin looks wrong to her. She remembers the strange, immediate certainty that something is very bad. She can still picture the drive to the hospital in fragments: red lights, the feel of the steering wheel under sweating hands, her son’s body too still in the back seat, and the sound of herself saying his name over and over in a voice she does not recognize.

The hospital is where time breaks apart for her. She remembers the fluorescent lighting, the alarms, the quick choreography of staff moving around the bed. She remembers being asked questions she cannot properly answer. Had he eaten? When did the fever start? Was there any history of this? She feels, in those moments, that she is failing an exam on the most important subject of her life. When doctors begin speaking in urgent, clipped sentences, she watches their faces for clues and starts bracing for the possibility that he may die. That expectation lodges in her body before she has words for it.

During his hospitalization she barely leaves his room. She sleeps sitting up, if she sleeps at all. Every monitor sound trains her attention. Even after nurses reassure her, she studies his chest to make sure it is still rising. She stops trusting absence of danger; if things can turn so quickly, then calm must be temporary, maybe deceptive. Family members tell her to eat, to rest, to “stay positive,” but she feels she has crossed into a different world from theirs, one ruled by numbers, lab results, oxygen levels, and waiting. She becomes intensely practical. She charges devices, answers messages, keeps lists, repeats information to relatives. Underneath that efficiency is terror so constant that she can no longer tell when one wave ends and the next begins.

Her son survives, and other people experience this as the happy ending. She experiences it as a release she cannot fully believe. Even after he comes home, she keeps checking on him through the night. If he sleeps too deeply, she panics. If he coughs, she is instantly alert. She memorizes the sound of his breathing and notices tiny changes no one else hears. She says she became “the human monitoring system” in the house. At first people praise her devotion. Over time they begin to suggest she is overreacting. Their reassurance irritates her. She thinks: you did not see him in that bed.

Her marriage, already strained, deteriorates in the months that follow. She experiences her husband as too calm, too able to step away, too willing to believe things are fine. He experiences her as unreachable and controlling. They argue about ordinary things that never feel ordinary to her. A missed call, a forgotten medication, a child coming home flushed from playing outside can set off a rush of anger and fear before she can slow it down. She begins sleeping lightly, then poorly. When she does sleep, she sometimes wakes with the feeling that she is back in the hospital, her heart pounding, already listening for alarms.

At work she remains competent, which is part of why people do not grasp how much she is carrying. She logs into meetings, diagrams network failures, and speaks clearly about redundancy and vulnerability. Yet her concentration has changed. She rereads emails without absorbing them. A minor service disruption can provoke a physical jolt out of proportion to the moment, as if every system failure is linked in some way to the one she could not prevent. She keeps her phone visible at all times. If the school calls, even for something minor, her body reacts before her mind catches up. On days when she has to go into the office, she finds herself checking the clock repeatedly and imagining unseen emergencies unfolding elsewhere.

Now divorced, she manages parenting and work with a level of discipline that impresses others. Her home is organized, schedules color-coded, backup plans in place. She knows how this looks from the outside. Inside, it feels less like competence than a bargain with catastrophe. She avoids driving past the hospital when she can. Medical dramas, news stories about sick children, even the antiseptic smell of some clinics can pull her abruptly back into those first hours. She becomes quiet, then distant, then ashamed of how quickly she disappears into the memory.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the sense that the world she lived in before no longer exists. She used to assume that if she was attentive and responsible, the people she loved would mostly be safe. Now she lives with the knowledge that a normal day can split open without warning. She still watches her son sometimes when he is playing, healthy and noisy and completely absorbed in being a child. In those moments she feels gratitude and grief at once—grateful that he is here, grieving the version of herself who once believed that love and vigilance could protect against everything.
